name: Viktorija Čmilytė
milestone_by_age_26: Won the absolute Lithuanian national chess championship at age 16 in 2000, defeating multiple grandmasters, and was ranked FIDE world number one among girls by 2001.
early_history_summary: Taught chess by her father at age six, Čmilytė won the European Under-10 Girls Championship in 1993 and the World Under-12 Girls Championship in 1995. By 2000, at age 16, she won both the women's and absolute national championships of Lithuania, beating three grandmasters in a tiebreak. She was ranked FIDE #1 among girls by 2001 and won the Corus Reserve Group at Wijk aan Zee the same year.
family_context_summary: Only child in Šiauliai, Lithuania; father was a KGB active reserve officer of Russian ethnicity who headed the Šiauliai Chess Club and served as her early coach.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father Viktor Ivanovič Čmil was head of the Šiauliai Chess Club and coached her from age six through her formative years, providing direct domain expertise and structured training.
evidence_summary: Čmilytė was taught chess at age six by her father, who ran the local chess club and coached her throughout her early career. She won European and World youth championships by age 12, then the absolute Lithuanian national championship at 16, defeating multiple grandmasters. Her father's dual role as KGB officer and chess club head provided structured access to competitive chess from an exceptionally young age. By 2001 she was FIDE's top-ranked girl and won the Corus Reserve tournament at Wijk aan Zee.
starting_point: Born in Šiauliai, Lithuania to a KGB active reserve officer father of Russian ethnicity who headed the local chess club and an only child in the family.
current_position: Speaker of the Seimas of Lithuania (2020–2024), Leader of the Liberal Movement, FIDE-rated 2538; married to GM Peter Heine Nielsen with four children.

name: Gabriel Yared
milestone_by_age_26: Won first prize at the Rio de Janeiro Song Festival in 1971 representing Lebanon, and arranged the album Minacantalucio for Italian singer Mina in 1975, establishing himself as a professional composer by his mid-twenties.
early_history_summary: Yared was sent to accordion lessons at age seven and later studied piano and music theory. At 14, after his piano teacher died, he became organist at Université Saint-Joseph in Beirut, using the university library to study Bach and other composers. He obtained a law degree but moved to Paris in 1969 to study composition at the École Normale de Musique under Henri Dutilleux. In 1971, he won first prize at the Rio de Janeiro Song Festival.
family_context_summary: Born in Beirut to a family with no artistic background; his father opposed his musical ambitions and urged him toward a conventional career. He attended a Jesuit boarding school from age four and later studied law at Université Saint-Joseph.
parent_family_domain_summary: No family artistic background; Yared explicitly stated that for generations there were no artists in his family and his father insisted on a proper career in medicine, law, or engineering.
primary_early_advantage_tags: self-taught organist,École Normale de Musique,Dutilleux mentorship,law degree as cover
evidence_summary: Yared grew up in Beirut with no family musical tradition and active parental opposition to music. He taught himself by studying scores at the university library while nominally studying law. At 14 he became organist at Université Saint-Joseph after his teacher's death. Moving to Paris in 1969, he studied under Henri Dutilleux at the École Normale de Musique. His 1971 Rio Song Festival win and subsequent arrangement work for Mina (1975) established him professionally before age 26, though his major film career came later with The English Patient (1996).
starting_point: Born in Beirut, Lebanon to a family with no artistic tradition; father opposed music and pushed for a conventional professional career; attended Jesuit boarding school from age four.
current_position: Academy Award-winning film composer with over 100 film credits; based in Paris; continues to compose for film and runs the Pléiade Academy for young composers.

name: Vahid Halilhodžić
milestone_by_age_26: Was a regular starting striker for Velež Mostar in the Yugoslav First League and won the 1978 European Under-21 Championship with Yugoslavia, scoring 18 goals in the 1977–78 league season.
early_history_summary: Halilhodžić grew up in Jablanica, Bosnia, where he played informally near his home. At 14 he moved to Mostar for electrotechnical school and joined the Velež Mostar youth academy at 16, encouraged by his brother Salem who played for the club. After a loan to Neretva Metković, he broke into Velež's first team in 1972–73 and developed into a prolific striker, scoring 106 goals in 206 First League appearances for the club.
family_context_summary: Born in Jablanica, Bosnia; his brother Salem played as a striker for Velež Mostar and was instrumental in getting Vahid into the club's academy. Family was not wealthy; Vahid pursued electrotechnical schooling alongside football.
parent_family_domain_summary: Older brother Salem was a striker at Velež Mostar and insisted Vahid join the club's youth academy, providing direct domain access and insider knowledge of the professional football pathway.

evidence_summary: Halilhodžić grew up in Jablanica, Bosnia, playing football near his home. His older brother Salem, a striker at Velež Mostar, pushed him to join the club's youth academy at 16. After a loan spell, Vahid became a first-team regular in 1972–73 and developed into a prolific scorer in the Yugoslav First League. By 1978, he was a key member of the Yugoslav U-21 team that won the European Championship. His brother's insider position at the club provided the critical pathway into professional football.

He became a key player in the famous Metaloplastika generation that dominated Yugoslav and European handball, winning the World Championship silver in 1982 and Olympic gold in 1984.

name: Andrés Gómez
milestone_by_age_26: Won the Italian Open (ATP Masters) in 1982 at age 22 and reached world No. 5 in the ATP rankings by 1984, establishing himself as a top-tier professional tennis player well before 26.
early_history_summary: Gómez grew up in Guayaquil, Ecuador, where his father took him to the Guayaquil Tennis Club to keep him off the streets, placing him under coach Miguel Olvera. He dominated junior tournaments and represented Ecuador internationally as a teenager. He turned professional in 1979 and won the Italian Open in 1982, one of the most prestigious clay-court titles. By 1984, he was ranked world No. 5 and had won five tournaments that season.
family_context_summary: Son of Pedro Pablo Gómez Sánchez, a prominent radio broadcaster, and Vicenta Santos Alcívar in Guayaquil, Ecuador. His father directed him to tennis to avoid street football and hired coach Miguel Olvera at the Guayaquil Tennis Club.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a well-known radio broadcaster (acreditado radiodifusor), not a tennis domain expert, but had the social connections to access the Guayaquil Tennis Club and arrange professional coaching for his son.

name: Falco
milestone_by_age_26: Released 'Der Kommissar' in 1981 which became a number-one hit across Germany, France, Italy, Spain, and Japan, and his debut album Einzelhaft topped charts in Austria and the Netherlands, all by age 24.
early_history_summary: Born Johann Hölzel in Vienna to a working-class family, Falco showed musical talent from toddlerhood. He attended the Vienna Conservatoire at 16 but left frustrated. After military service, he played bass in Viennese underground bands including the Hallucination Company and Drahdiwaberl, adopting his stage name in 1978. His song 'Ganz Wien' attracted manager Markus Spiegel, who signed him as a solo artist in 1981. 'Der Kommissar' became a massive international hit that same year.
family_context_summary: Born to a working-class family in Margareten, a working-class district of Vienna; mother was a laundry branch manager, father a machine factory foreman who left the family when Falco was a child. He was the sole survivor of a triplet pregnancy.
parent_family_domain_summary: No family musical background; mother raised him alone after father left. Mother supported his musical interests with instruments (child's grand piano at age four, record player at five) despite modest circumstances.
primary_early_advantage_tags: working-class Vienna,Viennese underground scene,Drahdiwaberl,Neue Deutsche Welle,Der Kommissar hit
evidence_summary: Falco grew up in a working-class Vienna household raised by his mother after his father left. He showed early musical talent but dropped out of the Vienna Conservatoire. He built his career through the Viennese underground club scene, playing bass in bands like Drahdiwaberl before being signed as a solo artist in 1981. 'Der Kommissar' fused rap with German-language pop, riding the Neue Deutsche Welle wave to become a number-one hit across multiple countries. His mother's modest support (piano, record player) and the Viennese nightlife ecosystem were key early enablers.
starting_point: Born in working-class Margareten, Vienna to a laundry manager mother and factory foreman father who left the family; sole survivor of a triplet pregnancy; raised by his mother in modest circumstances.
current_position: Died in a car crash on February 6, 1998, at age 40 in the Dominican Republic; best-selling Austrian singer of all time with 20 million albums and 40 million singles sold.

name: Salvatore Schillaci

early_history_summary: Schillaci grew up in poverty in the CEP neighborhood of Palermo, Sicily, doing odd jobs as a confectioner's assistant and street vendor while playing for amateur team AMAT Palermo. In 1982, at age 17, he signed for Messina in Serie C2, where he developed over seven years, winning the Serie B top-scorer award with 23 goals in 1988–89. He joined Juventus in 1989 and made his Serie A debut at 24, leading to his World Cup heroics in 1990.
family_context_summary: Born into a poor working-class family in the CEP neighborhood of Palermo, Sicily; never went to school and grew up on the streets. He earned £1.50 per goal for his local amateur side before turning professional.
parent_family_domain_summary: No family football background; family was working-class and poor. Schillaci's passion for football kept him out of trouble in a rough neighborhood.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Palermo poverty,AMAT Palermo,Messina seven years,Serie B capocannoniere,1990 World Cup Golden Boot
evidence_summary: Schillaci rose from deep poverty in Palermo's slums, never attending school, to become the 1990 World Cup's top scorer and best player. He spent seven years at Messina in lower divisions before his Serie B top-scorer season earned him a move to Juventus at 24. His World Cup heroics at 25 — six goals, Golden Boot, and Golden Ball — represent one of football's most dramatic late-bloomer breakthroughs. No family resources or domain connections facilitated his path; it was driven by raw talent and determination from the streets of Palermo.

name: Georges Moustaki
milestone_by_age_26: Wrote the lyrics to 'Milord,' recorded by Édith Piaf in 1959, which became one of her biggest international hits and a classic of French chanson, reaching number one in Germany in 1960.
early_history_summary: Born Giuseppe Mustacchi in Alexandria, Egypt, to Greek-Jewish parents who owned a bookshop, Moustaki moved to Paris at 17 where he played piano in nightclubs and met Georges Brassens, who mentored him. He was introduced to Édith Piaf in the late 1950s and began writing songs for her. 'Milord,' with lyrics by Moustaki and music by Marguerite Monnot, was recorded by Piaf in 1959 and became an international hit.
family_context_summary: Born to Greek-Jewish parents from Corfu who owned the Cité du Livre bookshop in Alexandria, Egypt; a cosmopolitan, Francophile household where he learned French, Italian, Arabic, and Greek. His father permitted him to move to Paris at 17.
parent_family_domain_summary: Parents were booksellers in Alexandria's cosmopolitan community; the family bookshop provided intellectual and cultural exposure, though no direct music industry connections. The Francophone household facilitated his move to Paris and integration into French cultural circles.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Georges Brassens mentorship,Paris Saint-Germain-des-Prés scene,Édith Piaf connection,Milord 1959,cosmopolitan Alexandria background
evidence_summary: Moustaki grew up in a cosmopolitan Greek-Jewish family in Alexandria, Egypt, where his parents owned a bookshop. At 17 he moved to Paris, where Georges Brassens took him under his wing and introduced him to the Saint-Germain-des-Prés artistic circle. This mentorship led to his introduction to Édith Piaf, for whom he wrote 'Milord' at age 24–25, which became one of her signature international hits. His Francophone upbringing and the Parisian artistic ecosystem were critical enablers, with Brassens's mentorship serving as the primary acceleration mechanism.
starting_point: Born in Alexandria, Egypt to Greek-Jewish parents from Corfu who owned the Cité du Livre bookshop; cosmopolitan Francophone household where multiple languages were spoken.
current_position: Died on May 23, 2013, at age 79 in Nice, France; beloved French singer-songwriter who wrote approximately 300 songs for major French artists and had his own hit with 'Le Métèque' in 1969.
